analysis.one_liner: Lets U.S. manufacturers trigger withdrawal of tariff cuts and bans imports from countries with large trade surpluses with America.
analysis.headline: The bill attracted no cosponsors, sat in the Ways and Means Committee for the rest of the 115th Congress, and never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would give U.S. manufacturers and unions a fast way to petition the government to undo tariff cuts when a trading country keeps barriers up against American goods. It would also require an automatic ban on imports from any country that sells the U.S. more than twice what it buys from the U.S., unless a U.S. company gets a waiver. Both steps aim to shrink trade deficits by choking off imports.
analysis.who_benefits: U.S. manufacturers, producers, wholesalers, and the unions representing their workers would gain a fast new tool: any of them could petition Commerce to strip tariff cuts from countries that keep barriers on U.S. exports, with a decision required within 45 days [S3]. Domestic producers competing against goods from countries with large two-way trade imbalances would also benefit, since the bill directs Customs to bar imports from countries that buy less than half of what they sell us [S2].

how_it_helps.text: It lets domestic manufacturers, unions, and business associations file a petition to withdraw tariff concessions from a country that maintains barriers on U.S. exports, with Commerce required to decide within 45 days.

It directs Customs to bar products from any country whose imports to the U.S. exceed twice the value of U.S. exports to it for six straight months, aiming to shrink persistent trade deficits that the bill blames for weakening U.S. industry since 1976.
It lets U.S. firms apply for one-year waivers when a banned product is not available in sufficient quantities from other sources, so shortages would not be absolute.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers would pay through higher prices, since the bill forces Customs to ban goods from any country whose exports to the U.S. exceed twice its purchases from us — which would cover China and many others. Import-dependent retailers, manufacturers that rely on foreign components, and exporters abroad would face retaliation, as cutting off another country's sales to the U.S. invites countermeasures against U.S. exports [S3].

drawbacks.text: The automatic import ban is triggered by a simple arithmetic test — imports exceeding twice exports — regardless of whether the trade is fair or the deficit is even caused by trade barriers, so it would sweep in many countries and cut off goods American consumers and businesses rely on.
Blocking imports wholesale would raise prices for American consumers and for U.S. companies that depend on foreign components, and would very likely invite retaliation against American exporters.
Trade deficits reflect broad economic forces like savings and investment patterns and currency values; a bill targeting import flows does not fix those underlying causes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is aimed at a real grievance — decades of persistent trade deficits and foreign barriers that the record says cost American industry [S3] — and giving unions and manufacturers a formal petition channel is a genuine tool for domestic producers and workers. But the core mechanism is badly designed: a mechanical import ban triggered whenever a country sells the U.S. more than twice what it buys, with little room to distinguish fair from unfair trade, would hit friendly and unfriendly partners alike, raise consumer prices, and likely provoke retaliation. Weighing job protection against economy-wide price increases and retaliation risk, honest supporters would have to acknowledge the costs could exceed the gains.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Ways and Means Committee and its Trade Subcommittee for the rest of the two-year Congress and never came up for a vote.

narrative.text: Louise Slaughter introduced the bill on May 25, 2017, with no cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Ways and Means Committee, which sent it to the Trade Subcommittee, and no markup, hearing, or vote followed.
The 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, and the bill died with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Importers, retailers, and consumers of imported goods are better off, since the automatic import bans never took effect. The bill's fate also reflects that even most members who favor trade enforcement did not support a mechanism this blunt.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Importers and consumers of imported goods

for.name: Louise Slaughter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral, sent it to its Trade Subcommittee, and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Only one member, a Democrat, sponsored the bill; no other member of either party signed on and no votes were ever taken.

industries.industry: U.S. manufacturers and producers of import-competing goods
industries.note: The bill gives them petition rights to strip tariff concessions from non-complying trading partners and bans imports from countries with outsized surpluses, sheltering domestic production. Factory workers would benefit only if the protection keeps or brings back jobs, which is uncertain.

industries.industry: Import-dependent retailers and consumer goods sellers
industries.note: A ban on goods from surplus countries would cut off inventory for retailers that sell imported products and for manufacturers that rely on foreign inputs, and higher input costs would feed into consumer prices.

industries.industry: Foreign exporters with large U.S. trade surpluses
industries.note: Countries like China, whose exports exceed twice their U.S. purchases, would face automatic import bans until they negotiated, raising the likelihood of retaliation against American exporters.
